utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Monday, September 15th, 2008, and I greet the accused, the counsel for Defence, Mr. Stringer and his associates, as well as the Registrar, usher, and everyone helping us, notably the interpreters. I think Mr. Karnavas needs a few minutes for some housekeeping matters, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Just one brief matter. Basically, as I understand it, the week of the 29th of September, we have Tuesday off, so we would be going Monday, Wednesday, Thursday. Now, I know we did this last year. I don't know if our schedule permits it this year, but I think that it would be helpful to us if we could have Monday off and then go Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. It would be more convenient for our witness as well. Now, you're shaking your head, Mr. President. I take it that you've already considered the matter and there's a scheduling conflict. Well, I had to go for it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's absolutely a scheduling problem. If the witness comes on Monday, well, I'll be here on Monday. Then for Tuesday, we'll just wait it out, as we say. That way, your witness can go and visit the city. And we'll continue on Wednesday and Thursday. This is a very pleasant city. I'm sure your witness will be very happy to roam the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Assuming the weather cooperates. Thank you, Mr. President. That's all I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom, please. Could the usher please go get the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You should be hearing, in your own language, what I am saying. Could you please give us your name, surname, and date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Borislav Puljuc, the 22nd of April, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a job at the moment? If so, which job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I work as the manager of the Ekoplan company, a designing company. I'm an architectural engineer and I work as an architectural designer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before an international tribunal or a national court on what happened in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time that you'll be testifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not testified so far about the issue of the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia before any tribunal, and I appeared before a court only once on another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which court and for which case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a witness before the local court in Mostar a month ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the case about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It concerned a case from the field of urbanism in Neum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Let me give you some details on what will happen, as I do for everyone. You will be asked questions by Mr. Karnavas, whom you've already met during the preparation of this hearing. After this phase, which will take some time, the other Defence lawyers of the other accused will also be allowed to put questions to you, but this will be a cross-examination, either cross-examination or examination-in-chief, depending on the topics addressed. The Prosecutor on your right, only one will be putting questions to you during the cross-examination. The three Judges on the Bench -- normally we're four, but the reserve Judge is not with us as of now, so these three Judges can also intervene to ask questions during the examination. During the this hearing, Mr. Karnavas will probably show -- present documents to you. They're in a binder, and documents [as interpreted] will be put to you on these documents. Please try to be very specific in your answers. If you don't understand a question, don't hesitate to ask the person asking the question to reformulate it. Notably, if it's a Judge asking a question and if you don't understand this question, ask the Judge to reformulate the question. We will have breaks every hour and a half. These breaks are usually 20 minutes' long. That way, you can rest, the Judges and everyone else also can rest also during those breaks, but those breaks are only 20 minutes' long. If at any moment, however, you don't feel good because you're too warm, too hot, or feel uneasy, please ask for a break. Judges, of course, are available if you have any questions to put to them at any point in time. And, finally, you -- just a minute ago, you took a solemn declaration. This means that you're now in the hands of justice, you're the witness of justice, which means that you should not have any contact anymore with the lawyers until your hearing is up, is over. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And, again, good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. You're going to have to speak so we can make a record. Now, Mr. Puljic, you indicated that you are an architectural engineer. As I understand it, you're about to get your PhD in that field. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the University of Zagreb. I have already submitted my doctoral thesis, so actually I'm nearing the end of my doctoral studies in architecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, your specialty, if we can call it that, is on urban planning.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in view of the small market of architectures in Herzegovina, I am also engaged in the designing of buildings and interiors, although my specialty is urban planning and, in particular, town planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, in fact, as I understand it, in addition to your private practice, you also engage for the Federation, and if you could please tell us how so.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I'm the owner and manager of the private company Ekoplan in Mostar. We are quite busy working on many projects, and the project you're probably referring to is the physical planning of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is done by a consortium of three companies; IPSA from Sarajevo, the Urban Institute of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Ekoplan. Therefore, these three companies are currently developing the physical planning plan of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the next 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I warned you before we got here and I'll warn you again, you need to speak slowly and complete your sentences. So don't chew off the end of the sentence. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I want to take you back to when you first started, when you first got out of university. Could you please tell us what you were doing at the time? What sort of work did you begin doing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Upon graduating from the Sarajevo University, I started working in the Directorate for the Construction of Neum. I spent three years working there and was charged with administrative affairs of the municipality, but also in specific matters dealing with the town planning of Neum and the municipality in general. Thereafter, I completed my military service and then started working for the Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we move on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we move on to Mostar, and again I must caution you to speak slowly, you said that while you were in Neum, you were dealing with administrative -- certain administrative affairs. Could you give us the details on that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Directorate for the Construction of Neum was a company of quite a specific nature. Given that Neum is a small town and there was a shortage in engineers, we engaged in businesses which had to do with different fields. One of them was the conduct of the administrative procedure for the purposes of the municipality, which is something that we did. However, we also engaged in designing and the supervision of construction works and so on. We also discharged all the other tasks that we were given by the municipality president or by the president of the executive committee of Neum municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you specifically given any particular task of which you worked on for two or three years -- two or three months? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I was charged with a specific task, i.e., to develop the wartime plan for the municipality of Neum in the field I am a specialist in; in other words, in the field of urbanism and town infrastructure, I was supposed to develop a plan for the operation of the municipality in times of war and in times of an immediate threat of war. The municipality of Neum did not have such a plan, and there was an urgent need for it to be developed, because a commission was due to come from Belgrade which was engaged in inspecting these same plans across various municipalities. I was the one who developed the plan ultimately. It was, after having been developed, adopted by a municipal body, which then forwarded it for approval to higher-level bodies and is then stored by the municipality president and set aside until a need may arise to apply it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I'm going to ask you to give me shorter answers just to my questions, and I'll walk you through step by step. You said "a wartime plan." Are we talking about a defence plan, and if so, could you please, in a few words, tell us what is this defence plan?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: In the event of a war or imminent threat of war, or in the event of any natural disaster, the municipality cannot operate as it normally does. For this reason, it was very important to clearly designate the essential tasks and who is to carry them out. This entailed us to define these tasks specifically, because the municipality has to function. There has to be running water, electricity. Public utilities have to continue operating, albeit under new and specific circumstances. Any municipality has to be prepared for such an event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, after your three years in Neum, you went off -- you went to Mostar. Could you please tell us what you were doing in Mostar? And be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: In Mostar, I worked as a specialist for urbanism and public utilities in the Secretariat of Urbanism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I'm going to fast forward a little bit. As I understand it, at point one time, you were on the Crisis Staff for the Mostar municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what period?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: That was between mid-March 1992 and the time when the Crisis Staff stopped operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please explain to us how is it that you became a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. Witness, when did the Staff stop operating? It would be more convenient if we had the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact date. It is, in fact, very difficult to pinpoint the precise date when it stopped operating, since as the time went by, the Crisis Staff had fewer tasks, fewer resources, and fewer funds to operate. That's why I cannot tell you the precise date. I know that over time, the Crisis Staff was practically left without any specific function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But you must be able to say approximatively. You said "approximately mid-March," you started, and do you not remember at all when it stopped -- when you stopped working with the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Crisis Staff ceased to exist in early May 1992, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, could you please explain to us how it is that you became a member of the Crisis Staff, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Sometime in mid-March 1992, a meeting was called of the Assembly of the Mostar municipality. Since the war had already broken out in Mostar and there was general chaos in town, this session could not be held in the Congress hall or in the Assembly hall. For that reason, all the assemblymen were invited to gather in a shelter on the other end of town, where it was somewhat more calm and where the communications centre of the Territorial Defence of the town of Mostar was housed. Ex officio, as the secretary of the Secretariat for Urbanism, I was duty-bound to attend all sessions. That was prescribed by the law. That's how I came to attend that particular session. A great many assemblymen failed to show up at this session. Some had already fled town. Others were in the army. Still others were afraid. And it signaled the fact that the sessions could no longer be held as per normal. For this reason, the officials at the Assembly said that the Assembly should cease to operate in times of war and that, in accordance with the law, a crisis staff ought to be organised which would assume upon itself all the powers normally vested with the town authorities. In the Crisis Staff, some were elected and others were appointed. The president of the Assembly and the president of the Executive Committee were supposed to become members of the Crisis Staff by virtue of their position, and every party represented in the Assembly should have one representative sitting on the Staff, whilst bearing in mind the need to represent the ethnic makeup of the town as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. But you, in particular, you were merely, and I say "merely" because in a hierarchy of things - urbanism is not one of the most important departments or secretariats - how is it that you, as the secretary of the Secretariat for Urbanism, got selected?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At one point, somebody nominated me and Mr. Skutor to be representatives of the Croat people in that Crisis Staff. By a show of hands of the delegates who were present, we were elected onto the Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before we talk about the Crisis Staff, could you please tell us, just very briefly, what did the Secretariat of Urbanism do? What was its function and what were you doing, exactly, as the secretary of the Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The very name -- the very title of the Secretariat indicates its function. Its title was Secretariat for Urbanism, Construction, Housing and Public Utility Affairs, and Environmental Protection. The Secretariat busied itself with the issuing of the building permits, with the housing affairs, public utility affairs; in other words, coordinating -- or being the coordinator between the cleaning services, et cetera, various public companies, and approximately 70 staff worked for the Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you, as the secretary of the Secretariat, exactly, could you tell us what was your function?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I directed the work of the Secretariat, coordinated all the various tasks, and together with my assistants, I dealt with all the requests that we received from citizens, and we would receive between 6.000 to 7.000 various requests from the general citizenry per year, and of course we also had to coordinate the activities of the various public utility companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Puljic. Now, we're going to be going through some documents where specific dates will be noted in those documents, and one of them does show that the Crisis Staff was established on 12 March 1992. If you could please explain to the Trial Chamber, so they can get an understanding, what it was like in Mostar at or around that time that led the Assembly members to set up the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At the time -- or by that time, there had been a lot of shooting around the town. The town was also being shelled and all the public utilities had trouble operating. There was poor supply of running water and electricity. The cleaning services hardly did their job. The undertakers could not carry out the burials. Many residents fled the town, and at the same time there was a large inflow of refugees. In a word, chaos reigned in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For how long did this chaos reign until the Assembly decided to set up the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Chaos started as soon as the reservists of the Yugoslav People's Army came over from Serbia. That was the so-called Uzice Corps. As these trooped appeared in the streets of the town, chaos emerged, and this situation prevailed through to the time when the last session of the Assembly was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, when did they arrive? I mean, I think it's important for the Trial Chamber to understand, because my next question is going to be: What, if anything, did the state government do to alleviate the situation in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The state authorities, and I mean at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did nothing, while the local authorities were powerless. The local police was poorly armed and didn't have any powers over military personnel. When the reservists arrived, and I can't recall the exact date - I think it was in November 1991 - incidents occurred around the town on a daily basis that could not be contained either by the local police or by the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you spoke of the special Assembly meeting that was held. Where were the Assembly meetings normally held, which side of the town?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The Assembly meetings normally took place at the Assembly Hall, which was the municipality building on Marsala Tita Street on the left bank of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. On that particular occasion -- and when the special meeting was held, where the Crisis Staff was formed, where was it formed exactly? Where did you gather?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Roughly a kilometre and a half or a kilometre and 700 metres to the right of that building on the left bank of the river. Since the building could not be reached any longer, it was very risky to try and reach it, since the left bank of the river was rife with reservists and armed men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you meeting on the right side of the bank or the left? We have to be precise, and the record now says "the left bank." So which side of the bank?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: On the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Karnavas. You said "to the left," but the left is relative. It depends from where you look. Could you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a rule. If you're looking downstream, then the left bank is our left side and the right bank -- so the left bank of the Neretva is the eastern part of Mostar where the old town and the municipality hall are situated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Correct, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, at this special session, how many delegates showed up, do you recall, and what was the ethnic makeup?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number of delegates, but I know for sure that many of them were missing. As for the ethnic composition, I know that representatives of all ethnic groups and of all parties were there, even if it was just one member. But all the parties and all the ethnic groups were represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about on the Crisis Staff; can you tell us the breakdown of the percentage?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: It was agreed at the meeting that as far as the large ethnic parties were concerned, at least two representatives from each party would be included, and the second principle would be that each party would be represented by at least one delegate, regardless of their ethnicity. And in that way, they wished to provide both party and ethnic equality. It's true that some members, by law and ex officio, became members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, who became president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: By law, the president of the Crisis Staff had to be the president of the city assembly. By law and ex officio, the president of the executive board of the town also became a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm asking for presidents, so just restrict your answers to my questions. And who was that individual?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Milivoje Gagro, the president of the Assembly, by law took the post of president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me go back to your experience in Neum, where you indicated that you were in charge of drafting the defence plan. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber who was in charge of -- or the keeper of the defence plan in a particular municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The plan was kept in the safe of the president of the municipality in each municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You say "the president of the municipality." Is this the executive --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the municipal assembly, is that the executive or is that the legislative? So we have to be very precise on this, and let me be even more precise. In Mostar, who would have been in charge of the defence plan? Just give me a name.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Milivoje Gagro.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you told us that from sometime in November 1991, to your recollection, Mostar began having problems, and we know or we're going to find out that on 12 March the Crisis Staff was established. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber if and when Mr. Gagro pulled out this defence plan.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that he ever pulled it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's talk a little bit about the Crisis Staff. And we're going to go through the documents, so we'll see a little more bit more concretely what it was doing, but could you give us a short narrative exactly how this Crisis Staff operated and what exactly it was able to accomplish, if anything?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff functioned with difficulty, with a lot of difficulty, and it didn't function to a great extent. There was several reasons for that. We were not in our own building, first. We didn't have the premises to work. We were in a shelter. Second, all the municipal services, all the offices for social services, urbanism, all the municipal offices simply fell apart, because people were escaping from the left bank to the right, many people left as refugees, they left Mostar, some of them were afraid, so in the best case some of the offices perhaps found some small room on the right bank of the river and that's where they would just report as having come to work in the morning. Maybe 10, 20, or 30 per cent of staff would do this, and then they would go home or to cellars to hide from the shelling. So we didn't have a building, we didn't have staff. We didn't have the offices, departments. There was no financial means. There was no money for the Crisis Staff. There were no basic elements for it to function. At the very beginning, all it had was its authority. Some members of the Crisis Staff were absolutely passive and some were trying to do something concrete and to assist in resolving the municipal -- the city problems. The everyday situation made them do that. They would be faced with problems from citizens and the directors of public utilities, who would come to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, who were the passive members and who were the ones who were trying to do something concrete?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The president of the Crisis Staff was passive. As for the public utilities and their problems, and I think that was the basic job of the Crisis Staff, Ismet Hadziosmanovic and Zijad Demirovic were also passive, while some members were really attempting to help the citizens to set up some kind of order, and these were Andrija Skobic, Josip Skutor, Jole Musa and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could you please describe to the Trial Chamber the assistance that the Crisis Staff for the Mostar municipality received from the state, from the state government or the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any contact with --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... come to visit? He was the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he send any representatives over there to see how the folks in Mostar were doing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: No one officially ever came from the central organs of power, although I must say that in a brief period of time, two or three or perhaps five or six days, within that period two people appeared who introduced themselves as representatives of the republican police administration. They showed their IDs. So it was the republic-level police, but I think that they were just escaping from Sarajevo. And they were there for a few days, they kind of wandered around, and then they disappeared. In any case, there was no official connection between us or anyone in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did the Crisis Staff ever try to mobilise the citizens of the Mostar municipality to sort of establish some sort of a territorial defence, something to defend the city?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The municipality cannot carry out mobilisation, although there is an office there for defence, but that office can carry out a mobilisation only pursuant to orders from military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you know whether any military organs issued such authorisation in order for there to be a mobilisation for the defence of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was there any sort of a defence organ in the Mostar municipality at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of the city of Mostar existed. However, it fell apart completely. We had no contact with any single representatives of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Mostar, because it simply fell apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were there any citizens of Mostar who organised themselves into some sort of a defence force?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The HVO existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we've heard testimony and we'll see some documents that on 29th of April, 1992, the HVO was given the authority to defend the Mostar municipality. If you could briefly describe to us, as a member of the Crisis Staff, how is it the Crisis Staff transferred this duty to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: We felt completely powerless at the Crisis Staff. The actual situation in the field was such that chaos reigned in town. The JNA was trying to occupy the whole town, and the HVO was trying to prevent that and was setting up a line of defence. Simply speaking, we had pressure from citizens every day to do something. Since there was no territorial defence and since the civilian police was absolutely powerless to act, the only solution was to ask the HVO to take over the defence of the town, the defence of the citizens, and to defend their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did they do that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: They did. We just handed that to them. We asked them to do it, and they took that upon themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we also know that a decision was issued on the 15th of May, 1992, that dismantled the Crisis Staff, and could you please explain to us -- I know you touched a little bit on that with Judge Trechsel's question, but could you please tell us: By that point, because we've also heard testimony here, the very first witness, I believe, it was Mr. Pejanovic, first or second, that the east side had fallen on the 13th of May, 1992, but could you please tell us what exactly the Crisis Staff is doing and what is happening in Mostar so the Trial Chamber can have a very clear understanding of the situation there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: There was fighting in Mostar, and the Crisis Staff simply had no function. We stopped meeting. Every member of the Crisis Staff started to worry about their own fate, and the Crisis Staff didn't have any force any longer to act or do anything in town. It could be said, thus, that already by May 1992, early May, we did not undertake any activities. The situation in the town was worse and worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just very briefly, because we need to get into the documents, if you could tell us, after the dismantling of the Crisis Staff, what if anything did you do? What was your involvement in and around the Mostar municipality following the dismantling of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: There was never a formal dismantling of the Crisis Staff. We didn't hold a meeting to that effect. Before we actually never met again in that function, we already had started to take up other duties. After the Crisis Staff, for example, I started to -- began in the Special Purposes Council of the HVO, together with some other colleagues, so the HVO staff of the city of Mostar formed a body, a kind of council, and assigned certain tasks to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this special-purpose council?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The main purpose was to use the authority and the cadre potential of the people in the council to start -- or to try to secure for the HVO material funds or financial means for their activities. This means that the council comprised people who had business connections, who were able to assist to procure equipment, and so on and so forth, so that the HVO could function more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the HVO we're speaking of is now this military force that has been given the authority to defend the city; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the military, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long did this special-purpose council last?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: We met two or three times. After that, we began to work individually. If I look at it, perhaps our collective work lasted a month or two. After that, we all worked on an individual basis. We did what we were able to, what we knew how to do for the needs of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was there some sort of a president of this council, was there some sort of hierarchy? Was there a statute that set out how it was to work and whom they were supposed to report to? Could you help us out here?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: We only worked on the basis of what was written in the decision on our establishment, meaning that we were supposed to use our business connections and to try, out of the Herzegovina territory, to find any kinds of support, including financial means, for the assistance of the HVO. At the time, the three of us, Neven Tomic, Jadranko Prlic, and myself were leading in efforts to do this, but really we all worked more or less on an equal basis and cooperated together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, after your work with the special-purpose council, did you do anything else in the Mostar municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Well, no. The municipality didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, once the -- at some point, however, we will see documents that they began -- there was some sort of an executive authority that was put in place to take care of the day-to-day functions of the municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period, there was pressure from the citizens who had all of these problems regarding public utilities. There was pressure on the army. For example, if the utility that is in charge of cleaning the town doesn't have any fuel and cannot get it from the municipality, then it exerts pressure on the army. If the undertakers' services in the city have no possibility to carry out their job and they don't have anyone else to go to, they will go to the military. So the pressure in this sense was quite considerable on the military, and they were unable to do their proper jobs because of it, whereas in the municipality there was no way that anybody could resolve these problems, the problems of the citizens who remained in Mostar and also the refugees who came to Mostar. The municipality was not able to deal with their problems, their issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So what happened?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Then the HVO set up some sort of local city administration, and that is when those problems began to be resolved in that body, easing the pressure on the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you involved in any capacity with this new city administration, if we want to call it that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. The public enterprise for construction and reconstruction of Mostar was formed, and I was the director of that company, and I began to work in that company. This was a publicly-owned company. It was owned by that local administration, the civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, what exactly did this company do? Just, you know, give us a general picture.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The enterprise comprised a number of prewar companies, including the Prostor public company that dealt with physical and town planning, then also the Dom prewar public company which dealt with the housing issues of the municipality, also the Public Parks and Recreation Service that maintained all the green spaces, also the public utilities/maintenance company dealt with issues of water, electricity and so on, and the -- and the business premises fund. So all of these different functions of these companies were transferred to this main company that took over all of these duties, and the concentration was necessary because a large number of personnel had left all of these prewar companies - some became refugees, some went to the army, there wasn't enough staff - so we needed to just put all these resources together into this one company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, I have listened to the answers you've just provided to the questions that were put to you in order to understand the situation, because the situation is indeed very complex. While I was listening to you, I got the impression that under the communist regime of the former Yugoslavia, there were various public entities, public companies, and you've just mentioned the functions of such entities. From what you've been saying, it seems that at some stage Serb reservists arrived in November 1991, and one gets the impression that general chaos ensued, that the municipality doesn't work anymore. Some people leave, elected representatives among them. That's what you said. And there is the general chaos. It seems that there's also combat operations. And then in order to address this situation, if I understood correctly, but if I'm mistaken, please let me know, the HVO then tries to remedy all those problems and shortcomings, and will set up a general enterprise, so to speak, comprised of various companies from different sectors in order to revive the local economy. Now, is my understanding correct? Is this the situation you were faced with? Everything was working under the communist regime. Then the Serb reservists arrived in November 1991. Then problems started, all structures disappeared, there's hardly any state left, and the HVO will try and address the situation as it was at the time? Is this a correct understanding? Is my summary of the situation correct? And as I said, if I am mistaken, please rectify the situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you are correct. All I would like to do is just to make one small remark. While the shells were dropping and while our town was being destroyed in front of our eyes, while buildings were burning, I remembered one lesson from university, how the engineers in Rotterdam during the World War II, while that town was being destroyed, while buildings were being damaged and destroyed by bombs dropped from planes, they were designing those same buildings, so my idea was that we have to be prepared once peace comes. If we were unable to restore the buildings as the bombs were dropping, we can at least design new ones in their place. And I suggested this to Mr. Jadran Topic, and he said that I should write a decision that would enable me to mobilise engineers to work on this job, and at the same time we prevented them from going to the army, from having to go to the front. And they began to design buildings to restore the town. They began to dream of peace and to dream of a new town more beautiful than it was before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in your own area you'd designed reconstruction plans. What was being destroyed under your own eyes, I guess were not the only one. I guess there were other people, just like you, who wanted to rebuild and go on living. But what you were trying to do, was it in response to the situation or what you were trying to do, was it based on ideology? In other words, were you faced with an extreme situation or was it all part of an overall plan? I know this is a complicated question, but I'm sure you'll manage to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my understanding of your question is correct, then this is my answer: Our activities, including mine, and when I say "our activities," I wish to say that more than 120 engineers were found by me over the course of a couple of days to work on this, our activities were not either ideological or ethnic based at that moment, national. What we wanted at that point was merely to be useful. We had expertise, and we wanted to put it to some use, rather than sit on our hands. We were not ideologically motivated. This can best be viewed through the composition of the group of people who worked on this, and through what we were doing, and through the first series of seminars which discussed how the reconstruction should unfold, and these seminars were held. As soon as the company was set up. We even had the president of the Party for Democratic Change, formally the Communist Party, among our ranks. He was one of the participants in the seminar who spoke of what the future of our town should look like. In other words, the company had representatives of all different political party platforms, representatives of various parties or all of the political parties who were once represented in the town assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you had all different nationalities as well, correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. At that point, nobody was concerned with an individual's ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us, how long did this public enterprise last?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: It lasted all the way until four or five months ago, when it went bankrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And for how long were you engaged with this public enterprise?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I worked in the public enterprise until the European administration was introduced in Mostar; in other words, until the arrival of Mr. Kosnik [phoen], when I was appointed deputy president of the HVO. That was Mr. Mijo Brajkovic who was president of the HVO at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you give us a month and a year, please? It really helps.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during this period, could you please tell us how many engineers, architects or other professionals you had working in this public enterprise?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Very soon -- at the very outset, more than 120 experts, specialists of the field, became active in the company. We were very busy all the way until early 1993, when due to the fact that the situation in the town grew more complex, we suffered an outflow of personnel, and our numbers were reduced, but the number of individuals active in the company was never smaller than 50 or 60 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us how this public enterprise was financed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't financed at all. There was no money. In the beginning, people worked on a voluntary basis and did not expect any remuneration. I managed to make sure that the people who were involved in the company received the collective humanitarian aid. I obtained it from the Caritas, and thus, in that early period they in fact worked in the company in exchange for a small bag of food stuffs that came as part of the humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. As far as the projects, though, where did the money come -- who was financing the projects which this public enterprise was involved in?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: There was no money. We received all sorts of aid, for instance. For instance, from the Konstruktor company in Split, we received the equipment for drafting, computers, and so on and so forth. When it came to the stage of specific works, we wielded our authority and approached various companies that still had different materials in stock in warehouses throughout the town, and that's how we managed to work. What we provided, however, was primarily specialist engineering assistance or counselling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. These companies that you speak of, were they privately-owned companies or are they socially-owned companies, not to be mistaken with public enterprises? And I'm sure you're going to help us out here.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: They were all socially-owned companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please inform us a little bit about the distinction between a public enterprise and a socially-owned enterprise or socially-owned company?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The owner of a public company is the state. Keeping in mind the peculiar nature of the Yugoslav system, in theory the owner of a socially-owned company are the workers employed in that company, together with the community at large. In other words, we had the right to take away something from the community in order to give it back to the community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I take it the Trial Chamber is clear with the answers, so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just very briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the answer is not very clear, Witness. You're saying that theoretically the owner of the socially-owned enterprise is the worker of that enterprise and all the workers of that enterprise. I can't really make sense of this. A socially-owned company, that's a public company is headed by the state. It's not the workers in that company that can head that company. They work for the company, but they don't own the company. So could you please tell us how it worked, because it's not very clear in our minds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are merely theorizing now, you'll appreciate. We are well aware of the fact that it was the state that controlled everything. However, in theory, the state owns public companies. The state sets public companies up and establishes governing boards run by managers. In socially-owned companies, workers elect workers' councils, who would then elect managers of the companies, and managers were the ones directing the company. Of course, the workers' councils, themselves, were being controlled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for these details. I think I understand now, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And earlier you indicated that it was the state that owns the public enterprises. At the municipal level, who owns them, and in particular the one we're speaking of? Is it the BH state or is it the Mostar municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, again, and this may help clarify your previous answer, the public enterprises, by and large in the former system, what sort of activities were they engaged in?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Public affairs, supply of running water and electricity for the benefit of residents, cleaning services for the town, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: To clarify something, Witness, you have said on page 29, line 4: "We are merely theorizing now. You'll appreciate we are all well aware of the fact that it was the state that controlled everything." After this, you explained what the idea of a socially-owned company was, but it's not quite clear whether this was more an aside and part of the theorizing, and that in fact, with all of these companies that you mentioned, all they were considered to be socially owned, it was in fact the state, that is the municipality, which directed it? Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not an expert in the field, but I lived in those times. Everything was controlled by the League of Communists. What we were discussing was theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Then I'm a bit confused, because I thought we were now talking of a later period where Mostar was practically in the hands of the HVO, and within the framework of the HVO it was that you carried out the planning and whatever else you did. And would you say that not much had changed in this respect since SFRY times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can understand it. It's a bit confusing, though. In the course of the examination, Mr. Karnavas has taken you through the times and we are now sometime in later 1992, I believe. The Crisis Staff has already proven to be inefficient. The HVO has been asked to take over the defence and is now generally the ruling force. And you work for them in the area of urban planning, and you say that you worked together with companies. The question then was: "What kind of companies?" And you said they were socially-owned companies. And then Mr. Karnavas asked you was it not different as compared to public companies. Then you said, well, in fact everything was ruled by the state. Now, that could not -- at this moment in time, the state, I suppose, have been rather the municipality of Mostar than the League of Communists or maybe the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we discussed theory, I was referring to the state of affairs as it existed before the war, because that's how the question was put to me. The public enterprise for the construction and reconstruction of Mostar was set up by the HVO. However, the purpose of that enterprise was to work in the interests of citizens. In its activities, it cooperated both with socially-owned companies and with other public companies belonging to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I will leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just as a follow-up question: By this point in time, had the state, BiH, had it been transformed from a command economy to a market economy?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At the time in Mostar, we did not feel that we were part of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina because there had been no contact with them, there had been no communication. The transformation was underway at the time, and it is still underway now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say "transformation," and "that is still underway now," you're talking about privatization of socially-owned enterprises and property; is that what we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, I must say that I'm a bit confused also about all this. Let's leave theory and go to practice. Let's assume -- let's talk about the public utility, for example, the company in charge of the electricity utility or the water utility. Could you tell us how it changed, what you saw as changes? I guess that the public utility in charge of water must have been controlled by the League of Communists at first. That's easy to understand. But what happened afterwards? Could you please develop using this example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The public companies at municipal level were set up by municipalities, and municipalities own these companies and control their operation. The companies on the other side have to report to the municipality, and they have to coordinate their activities with the municipality. The socially-owned companies worked on the market.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Water, who did it belong to? Did it belong to the socially-owned companies or to the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The water supply company, Vodovod, was in charge of the water supply, and it was set up by the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about electricity; was it the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the same applies to the electricity supply, to the cleaning services, to the town landfill, to the field of urbanism and town planning likewise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one final question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One final question before we take our break and get into the documents. If you could tell us what sort of work this public enterprise actually did while you were with it.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The first task we had was to plan the future town development. Our second task was to coordinate among all the public companies. In other words, if a street is being built, then one company is in charge of electricity, the other of water, and the third of the street landscape, so our job was to organise all of it, to coordinate, and for all these companies to carry the works out. So our task number 1 was urbanism and town planning. Our second task was to take care of the housing facilities in town; in other words, flats, to make sure that elevators were operational in apartment blocks, that the roofing was intact, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, were you involved in anything else, such as fixing the bridges or actually building any facilities? I'm asking you to be -- to list, so the Trial Chamber can get an indication of what exactly you folks were doing, and then we're going to go through and see more concretely. Could you please help us out here?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: We operated on three levels. One level was of everyday, so to speak, housekeeping matters and wherever problems arose. The second level were regular activities, and the third level was the future. This meant that we were busy with repairing the damage to all the dwellings in town in order to make sure that there was enough accommodation for people. We also engaged in the designing and repairing of all the public institutions to ensure the work of the town authorities. We also engaged in the designing, planning, and constructing of infrastructure and with town planning in itself. However, at the time two tasks had the priority in Mostar. One was to make sure that people had adequate accommodation, and the second, to build bridges in order to connect the two parts of the town. With the approach of winter, our main task and concern became the ensuring of adequate heating for all the people. Other than that, we designed schools, health centres, hospitals and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just one more question. Was an assessment ever made by your public enterprise, and was there ever an occasion for you to compile statistics as to what exactly your enterprise did?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did that first, to ascertain what the state of affairs was, and on that basis we made the plan of future activities, and of course we prioritized.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to add, it's still more than five minutes, so we're in no hurry in that respect. Witness, what is not quite clear to me still is the relationship between the planning, which is clearly what you were doing, and the execution of actual physical work. I had the feeling that you were telling us that your group did the planning, the organising, the coordination, but it was other entities, public companies of different kinds, and even socially-owned companies, that actually did the building, the repairing of elevators, of water conduct and whatever. Did I understand that correctly or did you have your own construction company, as it were, with bulldozers and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had engineers only. They were consultants engaged in all the various activities you've just mentioned. We were not a construction company executing works, as such. We would try and be resourceful and rise up to the challenges of a given situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So in modern terms, you did the software and you left the hardware to others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think we can have a break now, 20-minute break, and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Karnavas, you've used almost an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Puljic, there's your binder, and we're going to go through these documents. I would most appreciate it if you were brief with your answers. Only answer the question, and speak a little slower for the interpreters. Okay? Can you do that for me? Okay, thank you. All right. Let's look at the first document, P00135. That's your first document. It's dated 12 March 1992, and we see that it's signed by Milivoje Gagro, and he is -- at that point in time he's the president of the Mostar municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you recognise the session that is being discussed here on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I recognise a summons to a meeting. The agenda is the situation in the town, and lawyers recommended at the meeting that the time was ripe to abolish the Assembly and to form the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And do you recall -- well, let's look at agenda item number 2, where it talks about resigning of chiefs of security service centres of regions and of municipality. What are they talking about, when it says "security service centres"?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: CSB means "Security services centre," and it's the police. Since they were unable to control the situation in the streets, the chief of police resigned or wished to resign.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, are they military police or civilian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Civilian police. But you need to know that the civilian police has no authority whatsoever over the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Are you talking about the civilian police have no authority over military personnel, soldiers? That's what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Do you recall where this session was held, because we see here that it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A previous question, Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry, there is no address here, but it can be taken, I think, from the opening paragraph that this is addressed to members of the Municipal Assembly. Were you -- witness, were you a member of the Municipal Assembly at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not a member of the Municipal Assembly, but by law and ex officio, I had to attend every meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did you receive this convocation? Was it addressed also to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would always receive all the invitations or summons for the Municipal Assembly meetings in the Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you recall attending this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know where the meeting was actually held?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The meeting was held at the shelter in -- in a shelter at the top of the avenue where the TO Mostar communications centre was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, again, why was it held there, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Because members of the Assembly did not feel safe in the large conference room of the Municipal Assembly building where they were summoned to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, well, I guess, one last question. What, if anything, happened at that particular meeting, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Two things happened at the meeting. The Assembly was dismissed or dismantled, and its function was taken over by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 01635, 1D 01635, and here we see these are minutes of the first meeting of UNPROFOR delegation and the Crisis Staff, Mostar municipality, and this is 27 April 1992. Having looked at this, I don't know -- I note that your name is not mentioned at all. Do you know whether you attended this meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I didn't attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you at any point in time become familiar with the events or the matters that were discussed at this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: During the events, in conversations with Mr. Filipovic, who was in charge of that area and who had the information, I then did become familiar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. At that point in time, could you please tell us how many armed forces, armed troops, soldiers, whatever you want to call them, of UNPROFOR were there, you know, in the Mostar municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At the time, there were observers in the municipality of Mostar. I didn't see any armed UN forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to page number 2 on this, I don't know if it is on page number 2 in your document, but at one point the UN says -- the UN representative, that he heard on the radio that 100.000 to 160.000 people have fled from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you -- do you know whether that figure more or less represents the facts at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if that figure more or less represents the fact at the time, we're talking about 100.000 to 160.000 people who supposedly fled from Bosnia and Herzegovina, I guess that this figure comprises citizens from Mostar. Do you think that this figure comprises people from Mostar who may have fled from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very difficult to speak about the figures. I cannot give you the exact indicators. I do know that at the time, there was an exodus from Mostar. My family had already left, and the families of all of my friends, the wives and children, were out of town already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My problem is the following. I'll explain it to you, and I think my question is indeed at the very heart of our discussions. There is a Serb offensive. There is chaos. You already described the situation. There are bombings. To your knowledge, at that stage did people from Mostar choose to leave Mostar rather than hiding in their cellars to avoid being killed by Serb shelling? To your knowledge, did some people leave at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, people were already leaving town at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So people left the town. Among those people, were there any Muslims who were living in West Mostar or East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Women and children were mostly fleeing, Muslim women and children too, primarily. Yes, women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give us a ballpark figure? I'm talking about the number of women and children, Muslims, who left Mostar at that time, or don't you have any ballpark figure to give us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That number changed from day to day, from hour to hour. It's very hard to speak about numbers at such times. The first figures we received, when we began to review the number of apartments in the town and the number of people in town, and this was in June, after the left bank was liberated, it's very difficult to say, because the situation changed from hour to hour. Women and children first who had relatives in Western Herzegovina went to Western Herzegovina first, and then after Western Herzegovina was shelled and bombed, all of them went to Dalmatia. And then people of all ethnic groups left, both Muslims, Croats, even some Serbs who had friends in Dalmatia, or those who were in mixed marriages. But the majority of Serbs went to the other side also when -- as they were fleeing the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you can't give us a specific figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Before we leave this document, if we go to the third page, on the top of the -- the third page in English, there's a discussion here where Gagro says that, "Those are huge problems for us, and it will become increasingly difficult to meet the basic needs of the population. I must particularly stress that the aluminium complex has been almost destroyed by the JA." And then later on in the following paragraph, he says: "That is why I urge to do something to stop the looting of the aluminium complex." Could you please describe to the Trial Chamber whether Mr. Gagro is accurate when he's talking about the difficulty in feeding -- in meeting the basic needs of the population and, secondly, the importance, if any, of the aluminium complex?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's speaking the truth. He knows exactly what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about the aluminium complex; why is that important, if it is?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The bulk of the town lives from the complex. That is the source of our income. Watching television, we had the experience of Sibanik [phoen], where the aluminium complex was completely destroyed by a single shell. That means that the aluminium complex is in a field in Mostar, but actually its heart is at the transformer station in Subac. So one shell can destroy the entire complex, the entire facility, if you should destroy the source of electricity. So the aluminium complex can only be closed down according to a specifically-set technological process. If you don't do it according to that process, it's destroyed forever. So Mr. Gagro here is trying to maintain the electricity supply for the aluminium complex so that it could be shut down properly and saved for the future, because the JNA had taken over the transformer station of Cule and did not allow it to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the following page in English again, Gagro says that -- he says: "We are trying to negotiate with JA. We have offered talks without any preconditions. We are confused by this because they claim they are in favour of a dialogue, not conflict." Can you confirm whether, indeed, the Crisis Staff at the time was trying to negotiate with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then another point that might be of interest to the Trial Chamber. On the following page, the UN says that they have a second point, and it says: "This is the problem of electrical power and water in Capljina and Citluk. This is very important. The EC has already tried to assist in this matter. The transformer station, Cule, is between the two sides. I want a solution for repair as soon as possible because the situation in Citluk and Capljina is very serious and my troops will be deployed there." Now, the gentleman from the UN at the time was asking that there be repairs to the electrical power problems -- electrical power and water in Capljina and Citluk. Could you please describe to us what was the problem there? And, of course, he being from the United Nations, one would think that the United Nations would bring in the assistance as opposed to demanding that a solution be found, so could you please tell us what were the problems and what, if anything, the United Nations did, through its representatives, to repair these problems at that time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: UN representatives didn't have enough information about the actual state of affairs. It's evident here that their representative does not understand the situation locally, doesn't understand the priorities or the significance of the energy supply for certain facilities, so they did very little or nothing in order to improve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, finally, we see that the minutes were recorded by Ilija Filipovic. Could you tell us who this gentleman was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Ilija Filipovic worked at the business community. It was a public enterprise, and he was working in the Crisis Staff and the HVO staff at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are any questions, I'll move on to the next document, which is 1D 01903. This is dated April 28, 1992. Again, sir, I don't see your name anywhere. Can you tell us whether you attended this particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I did not attend that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if at some point you became aware of the discussions that took place during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I've already said that in my daily conversation with Ilija Filipovic, who is a good friend of mine, I got information about what was happening at the meetings between the JNA, UNPROFOR, the observers, and the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the very first page, we see a Mr. Skobic who gave a detailed presentation on the issues related to electric power, Energyopetrol, traffic, and economy. Now, one quick question. Have you had a chance to look at these meetings, and can you confirm to the Trial Chamber whether what Mr. Skobic is describing here is accurate?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything Mr. Skobic is describing is accurate. At the time, he was placing an emphasis on the energy supply problem because all the energy supply facilities were on the left bank. The right bank of the River Neretva in the town of Mostar didn't even have a single gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at page 2 for us, under item number 4, which is the economy. We see Mr. Skobol [sic], he mentions the looting at Sokol which caused approximately 200 million US dollars of damage, and this gentleman from the UN says -- I believe he's from the UN -- indicates -- Mr. Lundgren, he replied that he was aware of the consequences suffered by the civilian population, "all stated problems should be included in the report to Mr. Nombiar and the BH government should be approached over export issues." My question is: Do you know whether the UN ever got ahold of the BH government and whether the BH government ever did anything to alleviate the situation, as being suggested here?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the UN got in touch with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but the B and H government never got in touch with us, and it never issued a single instruction to us, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And the very last page, just for housekeeping purposes, we see that the recording clerk this time is a Jozo Kraljevic. Do you know who Mr. Kraljevic is?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I do know Mr. Jozo Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was his involvement with the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Jozo Kraljevic is a prominent citizen of Mostar, and he a well-known translator or interpreter from the English language. He very often did interpreting and also drafted the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next document, 1D 01904.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, before Mr. Karnavas moves to another document, I'd like to come back to this Mr. Lundgren. When he says that one should contact the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, one can draw the conclusion, by reading this document, that in Mostar there's no representative of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was it -- is it true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, there was nobody in Mostar who would be representing the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely nobody, none, none whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 01904, again these are minutes, 29 April 1992. Mr. Lundgren is there again, and I don't see your name at all. Did you become familiar at any point in time with this particular meeting as is being described in the minutes?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. The meetings were held on a daily basis between the UNPROFOR representatives, those of the Crisis Staff, and representatives of the HVO would also occasionally be invited to attend these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, there's a discussion here between Mr. Topic and Mr. Lundgren, and at one point Mr. Topic indicates that when they would have these ceasefires, the JNA would take the opportunity to fly over with helicopters to make an assessment as to what they had or had not hit in order to readjust their targets. Can you please tell us whether that was occurring, given the fact that you were a member of the Crisis Staff, also living in Mostar, experiencing the situation as it was occurring?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Helicopters were manufactured in Mostar. The JNA had helicopters, and they fly very low. But there was a helicopter that could fly at quite a high altitude, and it had a kind of strange sound. We would always know when that helicopter would be flying to record the state of affairs, the situations. We could tell it was that one by the sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at the next document, P 00180, P 00180. This is dated 29 April 1992, the same day that we had these minutes that we just looked at.
