We see this is a decision, and I'm going to draw your attention to the very last page, and you'll see members of the Crisis Staff and their signatures. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we can see under number 4 that is your name; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we were to look at the Crisis Staff, could you please tell us how many Muslims are sitting on the Crisis Staff at this point? Just give us the numbers or the names.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you read out the names, please?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Ismet Hadziosmanovic, Zijad Demirovic, Mehmed B ahmen and Fikret Bajric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And do you know how it was drafted?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I do. I drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. When did you draft it, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I drafted it maybe seven or eight days before it was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Why did you draft it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I saw that the Territorial Defence didn't exist. I saw that the police was practically not functioning. I saw that the town was being destroyed. I saw that the HVO was trying to protect and defend the town, and I simply wanted to record the existing situation and, in a way, give them the right and ask or request from the HVO to defend my town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, and we'll talk a little bit about the HVO in a moment, but could you please tell us whether, in drafting this decision, you shared it with any other members of the Crisis Staff, either while you were drafting it or immediately after drafting it and before presenting it for its adoption?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At the time, I cooperated closely with Mr. Josip Skutor, and he had all the information. A day before the decision was adopted, I met Mr. Jadranko Prlic and Mr. Neven Tomic, Neven Tomic, and I asked them for their opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How did you meet them? I mean, did you visit them, or did they come up to you, or how was it that they were involved in looking at your draft?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know why, but they had some reason to come to the shelter. They came to the Crisis Staff. When they finished their job, I asked them -- to speak with them. I asked them to talk, I showed them the decision, and we commented a bit on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you -- do you recall what sort of business or reasons they had for being there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. At the time, different people would very often come to the Crisis Staff and ask the president or one of the members to give them some work, a job, so that they could give their contribution to the defence of the city, and this happened quite often. People who had not been activated would do that, and they couldn't reach their companies on the left bank, so I assume that Mr. Prlic and Mr. Tomic, whose companies were on the left bank, were unable to actually get to their own companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And upon meeting with them and sharing with them your draft, could you please tell us what, if anything, occurred?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Neven said that he approved of the decision, and Jadranko said the same, although he suggested that I should add another article to the decision; namely, Article 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was that about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: He said that he believed it honest and correct to ensure equality along the ethnic lines in the HVO and that the command structure had to reflect the composition of the troops of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And was this decision discussed before it was adopted? Could you please tell us exactly how the decision came about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I requested, on several occasions, that Mr. Gagro should place the decision on the agenda and schedule a meeting for that very purpose. He kept avoiding to do so, and in the course of a morning meeting I took the floor and tabled the initiative to adopt one such decision. My proposal was accepted by all but one of the participants of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And who was that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Murat Praso, a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Witness. Let me come back to this document. It's important for the responsibility of Mr. Prlic. If I understood things right, you drafted this document, you created it on the 29th of April, 1992, you prepared this draft decision by which HVO and Muslim units are set up. It is said here that Muslims can have their own units. And you also state, on paragraph 3, that these units will be placed under a single command, the single command of the HQ of the Mostar municipality. And it seems that randomly, by chance, you just meet Mr. Prlic and another person, who are in charge of companies, and you're asking them for their advice. And Mr. Prlic personally asks you to add a paragraph, paragraph number 4, in order to highlight and stress that the command structure of the HVO must be -- must reflect the ethnical makeup. That's what you're saying; right? You're confirming this, you're confirming that this happened exactly this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why didn't you, yourself, think about making up this ethnical makeup where there would be an equal balance between Croats and Muslims; why didn't that spring to mind to you? Why was it that Mr. Prlic had to give you the idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, it is very difficult to be drafting decisions when the shells are falling. You can't keep everything in mind, and that's why we have the procedure in place where many minds, many heads, come together with their various suggestions. And had we had more discussions at the meeting, perhaps something else would have been added to the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this idea came from Mr. Prlic. Now, this decision number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't catch the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it circulated publicly or did it remain confidential? The number of the decision is 427/92. Was this decision published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I respond to your question, let me just make a small correction of what you just said. I drafted the decision five to six days before the 29th of April, and it was on the 29th of April that it was adopted. At that point in time, the Crisis Staff did not have a service which it used to have before the war and which was charged with publishing decisions. The Official Gazette of the local authorities was not being published, and that's why the decision could not be published. As soon as the decision was signed, there were two lawyers within the Crisis Staff, namely, Ilija Filipovic and another gentleman, who filed the decision in the archive. Upon the adoption of the decision, I informed Mr. Jadran Topic thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. By setting up these Muslim military units, things are clear here. You are setting up military Muslim units. By doing this, who did you think would be leading them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not set up a single military formation. I only established what the state of affairs on the ground was. At that point, there were, if I remember correctly, ten battalions of the HVO in Mostar and an independent battalion, namely, the 11th Battalion, which was mostly made up of Muslims. However, even that independent battalion of Mostar had over 30 per cent of Croats and, if I remember correctly, an odd Serb as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understood you right, when you were drafting this document in Mostar, there were ten HVO battalions and one independent battalion, and you're telling us, on page 52, that most were Muslims. And you're saying that for the independent battalion, there were only 30 per cent Croats, which means 70 per cent Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More or less, more or less. Very well. But in April, who was the military commander at the time, who was the number one in the military ranks in April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military commander for what, the HVO or the battalion, the independent battalion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the HVO and of the independent battalion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the independent battalion was Mr. Cupina, and the commander of its first company, or his second in command, was Karlo Deeba, a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We know Mr. Cupina. His surname is Suad; right? You see, I remember him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Suad Cupina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My memory serves me right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Prlic from before? I know that you knew that Mr. Prlic and Mr. Tomic ran companies, but did you know Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Prlic well. I was in the same class with him in the secondary school, and our paths crossed later on. He was the president of the Executive Board of the Mostar municipality when I came to Mostar. Thereafter, he was the prime minister or deputy prime minister, and I highly valued his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, if we go on to the next document, 1D 01905, this is April 30th, 1992. These are minutes with UNPROFOR again. And, once again, I don't see your name there. Is it safe to assume that you were not at this meeting, either, this meeting which was recorded by Jozo Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did not attend the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. In this -- in this particular -- in these minutes, there is a discussion about certain Klashnikovs going missing, and if we look at page 2, we see Mr. Lundgren actually suggesting to Mr. Topic that weapons be returned or given to the JNA. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know of this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, I mean, just so we have a clear understanding of what's happening at the time, is this a realistic proposal that Mr. Lundgren is putting on the table, in light of what is happening to the Mostarians at the time and of the JNA and those who were assisting the JNA and whatever they were doing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At the time, the people in Mostar were perishing from the fire of these same Klashnikovs, and Mr. Lundgren is suggesting that we give these Klashnikovs back to them. And I think he should have been well aware of the situation, being a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on to the next document, 1D 01060. This is now 6 May 1992, and we see that this is an order, and it's an order, and under number 1 it says: "To the Civil Protection Staff of Mostar Municipality to activate all civil protection plans for 'state of war'." Now, is this the same sort of plan that you worked on when you were in Neum or is this somewhat different?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Methodologically speaking, all the plans were the same, though everyone produced a plan of their own from their own field. The type of plan was the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But we're talking -- I believe that you had indicated that you were working on a defence plan, and this talks about a civil protection plan. Are they both the same? That's the concrete question.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: It's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did Mostar have a plan?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mostar had one such plan. Every municipality in the former state had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, under number 2, it says: "In case the existing plans are inapplicable to the concrete situation, to adjust and update them." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to your earlier testimony, you said that as of November or so, the situation in -- November 1991, the situation in Mostar went from bad to worse. You talked about chaos. We can see, from the previous minutes, that the UN is aware of the situation, albeit they're making some rather ludicrous suggestions, such as returning Klashnikovs back to the same people that are shooting at you, but can you please explain to us how is it that it's now 6 May 1992 and it's only at this point in time that we have this order to activate the civil protection plan and to look at it, at least, to see whether it's even applicable in light of the situation? Can you please give us a reasonable explanation that we can all understand?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The document says that the president of the Assembly knew of the existence of these plans. At the latest, at the setting up of the Crisis Staff, he should have gone to his office, opened up the safe there, retrieved the plan, and applied it. Where the plan could not be applicable, he was supposed to adapt it. The civilian protection had the plan, as did the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's be concrete about this. You say "the president of the Assembly." We're talking about Gagro, are we not?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to give you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In this respect, it's a bit strange that the letterhead speaks of the Assembly, which of course two months earlier, approximately, had already been dissolved and replaced by the Crisis Staff, and it is signed by the Crisis Staff. And so probably they used old stationary or something, but I think this should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll do that, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at the letterhead, it does say "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Assembly of Mostar Municipality," and underneath that I noticed "Municipal Crisis Staff." Could you please explain to us why we have this title? Why not just "Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Crisis Staff, Mostar Municipality"?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what else could have been written. That was only logical, "Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mostar Municipal Assembly, Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Judge Trechsel, do you wish to -- do you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why it's logical, because the Mostar Municipal Assembly, you told us, did not exist anymore, or was it only suspended on 16 March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The work of the Assembly was suspended, the work of a democratic decision-making body. Since it was necessary to work on a daily basis, the work of the Assembly was made more efficient and operational through the Crisis Staff, which consisted of a smaller group of democratically-elected assemblymen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: So that one must look at the Crisis Staff as something like a proxy of the Assembly, an entity acting for the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's why the president of the Crisis Staff is also the president of the Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Under the law, the president of the Assembly was the president of the Crisis Staff at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For further information, let's go back to the number of the order. It's number 958/92. Is it the number of the Assembly of the Municipality or is it the number of the Crisis Staff? This number, is it the number of the Assembly or is it the number of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the reference number of the document issued by the Crisis Staff. In other words, before this one, the Crisis Staff had issued 957 documents, letters, et cetera, and this was the 958th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll move on to the next document. This is a day later. This is P 00190, and here we see that the -- this is a decision setting up the special-purpose council of the Mostar Municipal Staff, and we do see your name at the bottom of the page, number three from the bottom of the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if we look at item number 2, it says: "The task of the council shall be to undertake the following for requirements of the HVO Mostar Municipal Staff." And then there are listed some activities. And, finally, if we go to the end of the page -- end of this document, we see that it is signed by Jadran Topic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, could you please tell us, on the list of the special-purpose council, are there any Muslims represented? And if so, could you please point them out?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are. Azir Sirko, Seno Kazazic, Veid Hakalo, and Camil Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And you did explain to us a little bit about what this special council was supposed to do, and I take it the activities that are listed under 2(a), that was your understanding at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're talking about the HVO Mostar Municipal Staff. Okay, what are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The Municipal Staff is the command of the army. The HVO was in command of the army at the Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then we see -- if we go to the last page, under number 4 we see that it says: "The work shall be coordinated through Mr. Neven Tomic, Jadranko Prlic, and Borislav Puljic, exclusively with the president of the HVO Mostar Municipal Staff, Mr. Jadran Topic." Can you explain this, why the three of you, and what exactly did you do in this capacity, you and the other two that are named?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Initially, we worked as a collective body for a couple of days. In view of the type of work we had, we started working on an individual basis. However, the three of us had to have all the necessary information forwarded to the Municipal Staff and, in turn, received tasks from the Municipal Staff which we were then supposed to carry out, in line with our terms of office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Concretely, could you give us some examples so at least we have an opportunity to figure out what, if anything, this special-purpose council did? Can you think of an example or two?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I can, but I have to explain the state it was in first. The HVO was the army, the armed people defending themselves from an aggression. These individuals, who had experience and business connections, had not been involved in that effort from the start. I asked Mr. Jadran Topic to get those circles involved so that with their experience and business connections, they might be useful to us. We engaged in various sorts of tasks. For instance, Veid Hakalo and I visited the business partners of Unis, a company where Hakalo was manager of, to procure boots. I know that Mr. Kosolic [phoen] went around in order to get radio sets. I know that Neven Tomic used some of his business connections to secure monetary funds to procure rifles, boots, et cetera. The purpose of it was to make use of the experience, knowledge, and business connections of these people in order to support the HVO logistics and to make the HVO more effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think there's -- at this point, I need to ask you one question, because maybe some may not understand to what extent the Mostar municipality was actually functioning. Could you please tell us about the other administrative bodies? Were they functioning? Were people showing up at work?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: First of all, the municipality had lost its building where it was housed. In other words, it practically didn't have a piece of paper. Second of all, many of the former employees of the municipality fled the town, became refugees. Many others became members of the army. All the services and agencies that once existed ceased to exist. There were only a few of them which managed to evacuate some of their equipment to the west bank, but not even they functioned. So the HVO practically didn't have the necessary resources that would enable it to work. Of all of municipal services, these were some ten secretariats, only the land surveyors had managed to evacuate their cadaster maps, all the other land registry office material perished, whereas from my particular Secretariat, only computers were evacuated. All the documentation and everything else perished together with the municipal building. Practically, we weren't able to be operational because we didn't have either the financial or the materials, resources, or, for that matter, human resources that would be able to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So I take it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if I were to ask you whether the banks were functioning and people could go and make transactions through, or whether the payment bureau was functioning, the answer to that would be, "No"?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's look at the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a second, Witness. Let's remain with document P 190. Take a look at the document in your own language. I'm trying to find a logic in all this. There is the checkerboard in the letterhead, and I see that the title of the document is "Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna." Underneath, there is the "HVO," and then underneath again one can read "Mostar Municipality." In the decision, there are four Muslims. You gave their names, four of them, and that's where I'm completely lost. Take a look at the title again. The title gives the impression that there can only be Croats, since it is the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna that's being referred to in the title. Within that Croat Community, there are also Muslims. I'm wondering when the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna was set up. One of its bases, was it a recognition of various groups; the assumption, was it that there would be Croats as well as Muslims within that community? Otherwise, how can we understand the presence of Muslims in that list? Can you please enlighten me on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is just one correction. It doesn't say "Municipality of Mostar," underneath. It says "Municipal Staff of Mostar," which means that this is not a municipality, it's still something that indicates the army. This is the HVO. And by this document, we are beginning to work for the army. We become members of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I was trying to understand if there was an ideological basis there. When the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was created, do you think that it was envisaged that within that community, there will also be Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, yes. This is what I sensed, I mean, how I felt, that it would include all the people who wished to live in peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, they could be Muslims, Serbs as well maybe, as well as people from other groups. In that Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, was envisaged to have various people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, we didn't view those things in that way. Whoever it was on the other side of the front and who is on this side of the front was more like it. So at that time, I didn't view things in that way. I believed that all the people should live in their own houses the way they want to live or the way they do live, and that they belong to that state and that country, the territory where they live. The Croatian Community, in my opinion, was formed for the purpose of protecting people and to enable them to live and function normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you're talking about the people, are you talking about various ethnicities? It is not the Croatian people; you're talking about a people comprising various ethnicities; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about all the people who live there, regardless of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last question. Let me quote you. You said that the HVO was the citizens in arms. I think that's what was said. In fact, the HVO was the citizens in arms. Are you talking about both Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The best thing would be to transfer that or apply that to my street. In my street, some Croats even fled. The majority of Croats obtained a rifle and joined the HVO. But a large number of Muslims in my street also were in the HVO units, even a few Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regard the Serbs, that's surprising, because they were fighting against other Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few, but yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I also have a question which refers to something that you have said sometime ago. You have started off the answer to the first of the questions of this series of the President by telling him that he had been wrong when he translated what here is "Mostar Municipal Staff" as "Mostar Municipality." You said that was not Mostar municipality, that was the army, that was the HVO. Does that mean that the Mostar Municipal Staff was actually something that was integrated in the HVO of Herceg-Bosna and not an emanation of an independent municipality? I wonder whether my question was clear enough. If not, just tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is my mistake. I'll try to do better. You said, after the President had asked a question: "I must correct you. It is not the municipality of Mostar, it is the Municipal Staff of Mostar." The Municipal Staff, you said, that's the army, that's the HVO. Now, my question is this: By stressing this, are you saying that the Mostar Municipal Staff is part of the HVO of Herceg-Bosna, of HZ-HB, and not an organ just of the municipality of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I wanted to say that a municipality is a territorial concept. If you say "assembly, municipal assembly," then we have the municipal and the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You may not know this, but we have here an ongoing dispute about terminology. Did you use the term "teritorijale" [phoen] or the term "podrucje", when you said it's a territorial concept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the Austro-Hungarian times in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina have remained the same until today. A municipality is a territory. The word "opcina" means "territory." But if you say "assembly," that means it is the assembly of that area. And if you say "executive board," then it's the executive board of that territory. If you say "municipal staff," then it is the military staff of that territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I didn't want to go there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But just to make sure that we fully understand, to what extent was there a civilian government working at this time in Mostar municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The civilian government could be said at the time wasn't really functioning at all. That could be said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas. I had not the answer to my question, which really was whether the Municipal Staff, Mostar Municipal Staff, was, in your view, rather part of the HVO of HB or still mainly an organ of the independent municipality of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Mostar Municipal Staff was an elementary part or composite part of the HVO. I'm sorry, I must admit I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Don't worry about it. You have not followed all our discussions, and we'll -- I leave it at that and take it for whatever. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether the president of the Presidency dispatched the army of BiH, for instance, to come and defend the Muslim sector of the Mostar municipality at this point in time, assuming that they were in existence?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At the time, there was not a single form of organisation of the state or the military of Bosnia and Herzegovina existed in the area of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in the Mostar municipality, were there Muslims who had organised themselves as their own units, fighting units, in order to protect themselves and perhaps others?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: They did try, but because they couldn't do it alone, then they organised themselves within or as part of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, one last thing, and we'll talk a little bit more about this, but the establishment of the HVO, and I understand that you weren't part of the military construct, but do you know whether that was put in place in order to Croatise the area; in other words, by that, ethnically cleanse it once the Serbs got through whatever they were going to do, cleanse the rest of the area of the Muslims so they can Croatise, introduce their language, their symbols, their school curriculum? Was that the -- to your understanding, was that why the HVO in Mostar at that point in time was established?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: No. The HVO never had the goal of ethnically cleansing the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to the next document, 1D 00909. Now, you have the original version or the version in Croatian, and if we look at the last page, we see three signatures, three names, one of them being Slobodan Lang. And do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we also have the date. This is the 11th of May, 1992. And if we look at the document, we see that there is a description of Mostar and what is happening in and around Mostar on the 9th of May -- 9th and 10th of May, 1992. Now, my first question is: Do you know Mr. Lang, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: On the 9th and 10th of May, 1995 [as interpreted], I met him in Mostar, and I spent time with him in that period in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, who is Mr. Lang, and where is he from?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I think that he's a doctor, and I think that he came as a representative of the Croatian government to see what kind of humanitarian assistance can be given to the citizens of Mostar and what would be the kind of things that could be provided as part of that humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In your contact with Mr. Lang --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must have been an error in the transcript. You said you met him on the 9th and 10th of May. This is line 25, page 66. And then we see "1995." I suppose you meant "1992." When did you meet him; in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how I understood. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In what context did you meet Mr. Lang?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lang was interested to see the situation in Mostar and what was the most needed, as far as humanitarian assistance is concerned, and what the problems were in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, since you were there on the 9th and 10th of May, 1992, having looked at these notes by Dr. Lang and the other two gentlemen, their description of Mostar, can you please tell us whether the notes -- whether the events as described herein are accurate and accurately reflect the situation as it existed in Mostar at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it accurately reflects the situation in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And we heard testimony, incidentally, by Mr. Ratko Pejanovic, and this was way back in May 2006. He told us that it was his understanding that the east side of Mostar fell on or about the 13th of May, 1992. Is that correct? You need to answer us so we can -- did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your answer --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... so we can make a record. Okay? And by the way, I'm referring to page 10387 from the transcript dated 5 May 2006. Now, let's look at the next document, which is a few days later, after the fall of the east side, that is, P 00209, and here we see a -- if you look at the end of the document, we see that this is signed by the president of the Mostar Municipal Staff of the Croatian Defence Council, Jadran Topic, and essentially it begins by sort of a historical context, if you will, in the preamble. And then we see that there is an order which disbands the Crisis Staff. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then it goes on to say, at item 2, that: "In connection with paragraph 1 of this order," that is, the disbanding of the Crisis Staff, "the Mostar Municipal Staff of the Croatian Defence Council shall form a civilian wartime government." And then if we look at number 3, it says essentially that until such time, that is, a civilian wartime government is formed, the special-purpose council will administer the entire function of the city and care for its citizens. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So let's go by order. Disbanding of the Crisis Staff. By that point in time, de facto, could you please tell us if the Crisis Staff was in existence and was doing anything useful, as it should have been doing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: We did not de facto exist at that time, and we were unable to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, how long had it been that de facto the Crisis Staff had ceased to be of any utility, if I may use that word?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I think some 20 days or even more than that before this date, the Crisis Staff was totally useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me go down to number 3, because it says here that a special-purpose council will administer the entire functioning of the city and care for its citizens. Question: Did the special crisis staff ever do that -- special-purpose council ever do that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Things were happening too quickly. That was the simple reason. So we never managed to do that, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's be concrete. In light of the makeup of the special-purpose council, the individuals that were involved, and we can see it's some of Mostar's best and brightest, was it in a position to carry out these functions, administer the entire functioning of the city, and care for its citizens? Was it capable of doing that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: It was capable of doing that, but they would have needed time and funds, means, to organise all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about at that point in time. I'm not talking about two months or three months or six months down the road. At that particular time, did it have the funds, did it have the resources, did it have the human resources, did it have the capabilities, did it have the security? Name me what, if anything, the special-purpose council had in order to be able to implement this part of the order; that is, administer the entire functioning of the city and care for its citizens.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: It didn't have anything that could be used as an instrument to be able to run or administer the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did anybody point this out to Mr. Topic, that perhaps he was being rather romantic, to put it nicely, in assuming that the special-purpose council could carry out these functions until a civilian wartime government was formed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't know who advised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, 1D 01987 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, I look at this document and I'm very surprised. This crisis -- the Mostar Crisis Staff commits sepuku, if I may say so. It decides and notes that it cannot solve its problems, it cannot solve any problem. Fine. So why -- why would the civilian government that is in the making would be more effective at this, because in this -- and this firstly there were Mr. Prlic, Mr. Topic, people like you. I mean, bright minds. So why does this say that others would be better at the job than you were? Why did they disband to create another structure? You're saying, "Because we couldn't make it," but what made you think that another structure would be better at the job than you were? I really don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "you," are you thinking of me in the position in the Crisis Staff or me in the post of the council for -- the special-purpose council?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm thinking of you as a person. You played a role at the time. I'm also thinking of others who worked in that Crisis Staff for a while and who, after Mr. Topic's decision, decided to disband the Crisis Staff. I really don't understand what the logic was. Could you please explain why you were passing the ball to another structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that de facto at that time, we didn't exist. We didn't have the instruments to administer. The Crisis Staff also had a number of incompetent men who at the time were not up to the tasks that they were facing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is incompetence absolutely everywhere. If you have to take incompetence into account, people wouldn't do anything. It seems that in a crisis staff, there weren't only incompetent members. It's not because there's a few incompetents that the job can't be doing. Why -- what made you think that the other structure would be better at that job? I really don't understand that. What would be the added value that they would provide, compared to you, your own structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not participate in the drafting of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you had taken part in the drafting of this document, would you have agreed with Mr. Topic; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said that I did not take part in the drafting of this document. I said this before. I'm speaking about this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, you didn't take part, but did you agree with Mr. Topic or did you disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not talk about this document. I did see it when it was brought to the staff, and it didn't mean anything to me because at the time the Crisis Staff was not functioning. It wasn't even at the first shelter where we were. We were at the cellar of the r ectorate, which was subject to shelling, and most frequently the cellar was empty. Everybody -- all the members of the Crisis Staff would be hiding in different places in town because the town was shelled on a daily basis. I saw that document when the messenger brought it and delivered it to the Crisis Staff which at that time was in a different building. We had already left the shelter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... nutshell, Witness, are you telling us that this is a piece of paper with no practical effect whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None, practically none whatsoever. We did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for the break, I believe, Mr. Karnavas. Let's have a 20-minute break. Thank you. We'll resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Puljic, are you with us?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I'll be doing my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. 1D 01987, that's the next document, and we see from the title that this is a report on the activities of the EC and UNPROFOR, and it's dated "Mostar, May 1992." And of course if we go to the page 17 in the English version, towards the last page, one before it, we see Mr. Filipovic's name again. Now, have you had a chance -- an opportunity to look at this report, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A couple of points I want to bring out. On page 2, if we look at the sixth paragraph, it talks about -- it says: "It was possible to conclude that EC and UNPROFOR observers had come to Mostar without any historical knowledge about our region, relations, and cultural, ethnic and other traits, and about how the former Yugoslavia had been created and why it had collapsed, or their knowledge about us was either modest or untrue. Maybe this can explain their indecisiveness, understatement, frequent suspiciousness, vagueness, and general inability to do what we expected from them." From your experience, being in-situ at the time, observing the EC and UNPROFOR observers, can you please tell the Court whether this observation in this report is true of the EC and UNPROFOR observers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, these observations are absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm running out of time, so I won't cover much of what is discussed in this report, but if we go -- in the English version, it would be page 14. It's -- it would be the section where it discusses the events of 12 May 1992. 12 May 1992. I'll just read a portion of it, and I'm going to ask you whether you can confirm this. There is a discussion between Mr. Jaganjac and Mr. Lundgren. Did you know Mr. Jaganjac and if so, who was he?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I knew him at the time and I know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At the time, he was the commander of the Municipal Staff or, rather, the Staff that was in existence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you're going to have to speak slowly, full sentences, and make sure to enunciate. Now, was he a Croat, was he a Muslim, or was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, here is Mr. Jaganjac says to Mr. Lundgren on that particular occasion: "I would like to tell you something. I am the professional here, an officer, while Mr. Topic is a well-known football player and Mr. Petar --" I suspect they're talking about Petar Zalenika -- "is it a well-known worker. The people are defending themselves here and the price is not important to us." Can you confirm to us whether Mr. Jaganjac had been or was at the time a professional officer? In other words, had he been with the JNA prior to the breakup or the events?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: According to the information I had, he was formerly a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Mr. Topic; was he -- had he been a football player by trade?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, a well-known footballer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. In fact, he had played for Kosmos; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes. He even played on the Yugoslav representation team, and he also played in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Petar, that would be -- would that be Petar Zalenika?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's Petar Zalenika.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what's his occupation? It says he was a well-known worker. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaganjac must have been mistaken. Mr. Zalenika was on the police force before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. Thank you, I have nothing more for this document, and we'll move on to the next segment, unless the Judges have any questions about the events that are in the report. If not, let's turn over -- let's go to P 00221. This is a Prosecution document. We've seen it here before, and this now is 21 May 1992. Okay. So this is a decision to establish -- for the establishment of the temporary executive power and administration in the territory of the HZ-HB. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I don't believe your name is anywhere on the list.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On number 12, we do see Jasmin Jaganjac, the individual you just told us, and he's the head of the Defence Department; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, so this decision essentially is coming how many days after the previous decision that we saw of dismantling of the Crisis Staff, which was May 15, 1992, and this is -- so we're talking six days later; right? Roughly a week?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. During that one-week period, I mean, you told us about the capabilities or lack thereof of the special-purpose council, but during that week or six days, were you able to do anything concretely? When I say "you," not you personally; the special-purpose council.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Nothing could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at this list, do we see any Muslims on this list for this temporary executive power and administration? And if so, could you please point them out?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are Muslims. Number 3, Mumin Isic, who was also a member of the executive board of the municipality, then Senad Kazazic, who had also had experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Please slow down, please enunciate. I'm trying to make a record.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Mumin Isic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... at the beginning. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Of the Muslims on the list, there are as follows: Under number 3, Mumin Isic; under number 5, Senad Kazazic; under 6, Sejo Maslo; under 8, Hamdija Jahic; under 12, Jasmin Jaganjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what did Mr. Isic do? You were telling us what he did before, and I want to ask you to just very briefly describe these various departments. So what did Mr. Isic do before?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Isic is a lawyer by profession. Before the war, he was the secretary of the Executive Committee of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about the next, number 5, Senad Kazazic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Senad Kazazic, I don't know his profession, but he worked in a municipal public company which took care of the maintenance of residences. Sejo Maslo had also worked for the municipality in one of the departments. I can't remember which. Hamdija Jahic had also worked for the municipality as the secretary of the Secretariat for Urbanism. He was my supervisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in what capacity were you working in the -- with the municipality for this person to be your supervisor, for Mr. Jahic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was coordinator for urbanism. That was the official title of the post. In other words, I coordinated the work of all the engineers in the Secretariat for Urbanism. I was a sort of superior of theirs, in a way, whereas Hamdija Jahic was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to the next document, 1D 00544, we see that this is dated 21 May 1992. This is a conclusion to proclaim the hospital in Mostar a war hospital, and could you please explain to us why was it necessary to pass this conclusion, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: In that time of prevailing chaos, the only body that was working was the HVO, and all the other institutions were trying to come closer to the HVO in order to be operational at all. The fact that the hospital was proclaimed a war hospital meant that it was now entitled to receive certain material funds from the army, including fuel and other resources, since the civilian authorities were unable to be helpful in any way. However, the hospital treated civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We go to the next one, 1D 00548. This is 29 May 1992. This is a conclusion. And it says: "All certificates or decisions allocating or allowing occupancy of homes abandoned by the previous orders without any valid reasons are hereby rendered null and void because they were issued by unauthorised persons." This is a sort of contentious issue throughout this trial. At this point in time, could you please tell us, why was it necessary to pass this conclusion, keeping in mind 29 May 1992, and give us a little flavour, especially for the Judges, of what it was like to live in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: There was chaos. The town was full of refugees from Eastern Herzegovina and displaced persons from the eastern quarter of town. People were out in the street. They had to find shelter for themselves and their children. There were mass-scale instances of individuals breaking into flats to find shelter. In order to introduce some sort of lawfulness in all of that, these individuals approached various offices, requesting certificates or permits. Now, in order to introduce order in all of that, it was necessary to invalidate all these certificates and to initiate procedures allocating flats to the people who were homeless.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. We go to the next document, 1D 02391, 1D 02391, and in the English version we need to correct the date at the top. It should be "2 June 1992," as opposed to "February." And that's what it says, does it not, in the Croatian version, "2 June"? Mr. Puljic, I'm asking a question. That's what it says, "2 June 1992"; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, this is -- we see under "Croatian Defence Council, HVO Mostar," we see: "To the special-purpose council." Subject: "Information on the food situation and need of the population in Mostar." And if we just look, I just want to focus everyone's attention to the second paragraph. It says: "We hereby ask that the food supply and distribution system in local communes be set up without delay through civilian protection staffs, particularly the distribution of bread." Explain to us, why was it necessary for this to be passed by the -- by Professor Skutor, who is the head of the Civilian Protection of Mostar municipality at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: He had no one to turn to. He needed to have everything that is the subject of his request, and he addressed the only institution in existence at the time; namely, the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'll move to the next document, and the next document is 1D 00563. And we see this document is -- all right, I'm sorry, I skipped a document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I skipped a document. We're going to be dealing with 1D 01572. My apologies. 1572. We're moving chronologically so that we can get sort of a snapshot of what's happening. And, again, for everyone's convenience, on 5 May 2006, Mr. Pejanovic had indicated that the east side had been liberated on or about the 14th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would that be accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the precise date, but it was in mid-June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in this particular document, we see that this is an excerpt from the speech from Commander Pasalic, Arif Pasalic. Did you know the gentleman, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I met him once during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, he talks about -- this is a speech that he gave on July 12th, 1992. We see that from the beginning of the text. Further down in the first paragraph, he talks about: "SDA and HDZ played a special role in the arming of citizens especially." And he talks about -- and he lists the individuals, Hadziosmanovic, Zalenika, Cupina, Slezak, Nozic and others. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The HDZ procured weapons, and these individuals distributed it, Hadziosmanovic and the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then on page 2, the first paragraph, in the middle of it, it says: "On June 14th, early in the morning at 300 hours, combat begins and the left bank is attacked. The battalion, together with the military police forces of HVO, fight the determining battle to win over the left bank and adjoining portion of the city ." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you've read his speech. Can you comment overall on the accuracy of Mr. Pasalic's distribution of the events and the involvement of those who liberated Mostar and fought for the liberation of the Mostar municipality?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Mostar is some 50 kilometres long from the northern to the southern boundaries. The town proper stretches over some ten kilometres in the north-south direction. Upon reading this article, one gets the impression that Mr. Arif and his soldiers were the ones who liberated the town, which simply isn't true. The town was being liberated along the length of the front line and with equal strength at all these points. He covered a narrow stretch of land with his soldiers. That was some 200 to 300 metres in width, if my memory serves me well. What is also noteworthy is that he said here that the first one to reach the left bank was Karlo Dzeba and his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me. Witness, you are written down here, on line 20, of saying that the municipality of Mostar is some 50 kilometres long. Did you mean 50, not 15? That's the municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifty, 5-0, from the north to the south.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're not talking about the city. We're talking about the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I said that the municipality stretched over some 50 kilometres and that the town proper stretched over some 10 kilometres. Arif Pasalic described the events on a stretch of the front line which was some 200 to 300 metres wide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So let me make sure that I understand you correctly. Are you trying to tell us that the JNA and their activity during this period of time, because you said that they -- as of November of 1991, things began to get out of hand, they went from bad to worse, was it not just in the Mostar city but it was -- covered the entire municipality, these events?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: Was the Crisis Staff responsible just for the city, east and west side, or was it responsible for the entire municipality and everybody that lived in it, all the villages, hamlets and what have you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: For the entire municipality. However, we had no contact whatsoever with those parts of the municipality, not even telephone communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you told us that it would have been the president of the Assembly who was then the president of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Gagro, who should have activated the defence plan, but never did so. Could you please tell us whether he visited the front lines, went to any place where there was activity, so perhaps he could have a firsthand account on what the needs were of the people and also what was happening?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that, and I never saw him tour any section of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one question I failed to ask you before. All right. Mr. Gagro perhaps was incompetent, or for whatever reason didn't want to activate the defence plan. What prevented other members of the Crisis Staff from going to the vault and getting the plan out, assuming you could get to the vault?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At the time, the highest authorities in the Crisis Staff were supposed to be Milivoj Gagro, the president of the Assembly, Izet Bajric, the president of the executive board, Ismet Hadziosmanovic, the president of the Party for Democratic Action for the region, and Zijad Demirovic, president of the Party for Democratic Action of the Mostar municipality. All the four mentioned individuals were passive in relation to the work of the Crisis Staff. They behaved as if they had been expecting NATO to appear and liberate them. Ultimately, when the liberation by NATO did take place -- or rather they would have wanted to divide power once NATO liberation came. The other members on the Crisis Staff tried to do as much as they could, albeit not much, to use their authority to improve the situation in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Getting back to my question: Other than those top four individuals, could other members, those who wanted to do something, those who were more engaged in the Crisis Staff, could they have gone to the vault and to retrieve the defence plan and maybe even activate it, against the will of the top four?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: They weren't able to. Even had they wished to do that, they would not have been able to do it without the four individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And correct me if I'm wrong. Of the top four, wasn't one of the individuals - perhaps you can correct me if I'm wrong - who in fact abandoned Mostar on a bus with women and children?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Fikret Bajric tried to do that, that's to say the president of the Executive Committee. He was on a bus of the UNHCR with women and children at the same time as he was discharging the duty of the president of the Executive Committee of the town. That was the talk of the town in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What period are we talking about because, I mean, there is this issue looming in the air that somehow there's a civilian government functioning called "Crisis Staff," so what period are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Late April and early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Finally with this document, do you recognise the publication of it? If you look at it, you have the original -- a copy of the original version. And if so, could you please tell us, what is this publication?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I recognise the publication. I think it was issued in the Vranica building, where Radio Mostar was housed, the radio which was controlled by the SDA. That was also where the municipal -- what do you call it -- the municipal HVO was housed with Mr. Topic, Jadran Topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. If we go to the next document, 1D 005 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to go back to something you said. You said Mr. Fikret Bajric left Mostar with women and children, in a UNHCR bus. When he left with his family, why -- why was he leaving? Was there any shelling by the Serbs or didn't he like the atmosphere anymore? Why? Why did he leave in such a hurry? Was there any particular reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that he left. At that time, I didn't see him any longer. But I think that he left because the town was being shelled and because the man wanted to go to a safe place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood well, whether you're a Croat or a Muslim at the time, the only thing you had to do was to go to the UNHCR, say that there were some shellings and that you wanted to leave, and then the UNHCR would put anybody who wanted to leave the city at their disposal a bus so that they could leave. Is that what happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The UNHCR provided buses primarily for women and children, but all those who managed to get in the buses would leave in those same buses. If they managed to do it, that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't notice this before. If I understand you correctly, the UNHCR had a procedure in place in order to evacuate the inhabitants of Mostar, given the war situation which prevailed at the time. So there were buses, UNHCR buses, in which residents from Mostar, women, children, but also maybe men, and then everybody would leave the city in convoys? Is it how it was organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And those who were leaving, were they leaving on their own free will or were they leaving because of the general atmosphere because of the shellings, artillery, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] People were trying to escape the shelling, so it was just a product of the fear of the shells and because of the shelling. There was no other reason to leave town at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were there, and maybe you're in a good position to give an answer to this question. To your knowledge, as far as you know, what was the percentage of Croats leaving the city and what was the percentage of Muslims leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same. It just depended on the courage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. In certain situations, you stay, and in other situations, even if you're brave, you have to leave. As far as you're concerned, what was the proportion of people leaving Mostar? Were 50 per cent Croats, 50 per cent Muslims, 70/30, or should we ask that question to the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it would have been better to ask somebody from the UNHCR. If you ask me, I have to tell you all my thoughts about that question. I think that perhaps a large number of Croats left because they had friends and relatives in Western Herzegovina, so they had somewhere to stay. I think that more Croats left Mostar at that time than Muslims because they had relatives in Western Dalmatia, in Herzegovina, and they had somewhere to put them up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Remember, you said that in the street where you lived, there were both Croats and Muslims, on your own street, so could you tell us how many left on your own street, whether Muslims left, whether Croats left, from your own street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were Croats who left and there were also Muslims who left. I think that at the time, the fact that somebody was leaving was not something that depended on ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 00563. This is a decision to organise supply of oil and oil derivatives in Mostar municipality, dated 19 June. Could you please explain, what is this about and why was it necessary?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: I already said that all the gas stations in Mostar were on the left bank, and the right bank, the western part of the town, did not have a single gas station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me make sure I understood that, because I don't believe I heard that before. Are you saying that at this time gas stations were only on one side of the town?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So one had to cross over the bridge to get to the gas station? If they were on the west side, they had to go to the east?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there were no bridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, what happened to the bridges?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: And just one more information. The reservoirs and the storage depots for the fuel were on the other side. All the -- not just the gas stations, but the oil terminals, the storage areas, were on the left bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: This is a decision to build a gas station on the right bank so that the right bank would have a fuel supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 00567, this is a decision to provide vehicles for public enterprises. Can you explain this decision for us? Again, 19 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Public enterprises of the Mostar municipality which provide the town with electricity and other services were left without vehicles during the war, and here Mr. Topic is trying to obtain vehicles so that these services could work, could operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you again, because I guess we can't hear this enough. Did those services work prior -- you know, in May, and if so, why didn't the Crisis Staff issue similar decisions?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: If they asked us to provide them vehicles -- I mean, if they were to ask us, we didn't have the money to buy the vehicles and we did not have the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But these public enterprises, were they working, were they functioning in May, were they functioning in April?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: They all tried to work as much as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00889. 1D 00889, again 19th June 1992, a decision on the establishment of the Mostar Municipal Department of Civilian Protection. What is this about? And should I ask: Why was it necessary to establish a civilian protection department when it should have been in existence already?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: In any event, there was a need to organise the civilian protection better, because that civilian protection was organised in peacetime, and during its activities during wartime it became evident that it was necessary to reorganise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, had it been activated prior to this point, the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it worked the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 00587, this is a decision -- this is now dated 30 June 1992. This is a decision to introduce a work obligation, and it says: "This decision shall temporarily govern the implementation of a work obligation in the municipality of Mostar." Tell us, what is this about? And in doing so, tell us whether this is an effort to Croatise the area.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What is the decision about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: This decision urges people who lived in enterprises on the left bank to go back there to organise the companies, to protect their property, and to try to organise any kind of operation or function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you say in your answer, we have in English, "people who lived in enterprises on the left ..." Are you saying people who actually worked, is that what you meant, not "lived"?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: Who were working there, who were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. The next decision, 1D 00578. This is a decision on setting up a central construction material depot. Why was this necessary? Again, this is 30th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC
utterances.text: At the time, people started to go back to their homes that were damaged. They needed construction material. And because of that, there was even looting of construction material. In order to prevent that, the HVO organised a central warehouse to prevent robberies and looting, and at the same time to attempt to distribute the construction materials according to priorities, i.e., to those who needed it more rather than those who didn't need it that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Witness, what you're saying is interesting. If I understood you right, there was a need to rebuild, and here I'm talking to the architect. So there was a need to rebuild, but those whose property had been damaged needed building material. They needed bricks, cement, shingles, et cetera. So a central depot had been set up, and those who came and got -- and people could come to this depot to get building material. Now, was there a register or something in this depot so that you could list whoever -- the name of whoever was coming to get, for example, five bags of cement, and the person would sign in order to acknowledge that it had been -- it had received five sacks of cement, or ten bricks, or whatever? Was there this kind of register?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was the service. There were also people whose task it was to do that, and they did that. The problem at the time was also because everybody was securing humanitarian aid through a direct line, and then what would happen is that humanitarian assistance in construction material would go to a village where it wasn't needed as much. So that is why the HVO began to introduce order in this area, to assess the situation and then issue construction material and make a record of it in order to prevent abuses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking this question in order to know whether there exists elements that could hint at the following fact, the fact that the HVO had set up a system so that Muslims from East Mostar could obtain construction material that they needed to rebuild their homes, in order to fix their homes. This is what I'm trying to find out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no tensions at the time, and there were no such intentions at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you've understood my question. I would like to know whether there are documents, like registers, that would state that, for example, that Mr. X, a Muslim from East Mostar, received five bags of cement to rebuild his house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
